claim: Anthropic's production multi-agent research system decomposes work through an explicit orchestrator-worker pattern: a lead agent analyzes the query, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents (each given an objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries) that run in parallel. Rather than pricing the plan before running it, the system scales agent count and tool-call budget by a query-complexity tier (1 agent/3-10 calls up to 10+ subagents), because -- per the same source -- 'Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so we embedded scaling rules in the prompts,' i.e. effort allocation is a prompted heuristic, not a computed cost estimate. Published Jun 13, 2025, older than this task's 2026-03 recency preference, but it is Anthropic's own primary account of a real, named production system's decomposition mechanism, so it is kept and flagged rather than excluded.
query: Quote the exact text describing how the lead agent decomposes a task into subtasks, delegates to subagents, and any mention of an orchestrator-worker pattern or execution pattern selection. Also quote any text about estimating cost/steps/token budget before or during execution.
read: orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. ... Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents. ... Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so we embedded scaling rules in the prompts.
snippet: the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously
title: How we built our multi-agent research system
topic: Production multi-agent task decomposition: Anthropic's lead-agent orchestrator-worker pattern and dynamic effort scaling instead of pre-execution cost estimation

claim: Amazon Bedrock's multi-agent collaboration -- a real, currently-documented, generally-available production offering -- implements the supervisor pattern with two selectable allocation modes: plain 'Supervisor' (coordinates and synthesizes responses from collaborator agents) versus 'Supervisor with routing' (routes directly to one collaborator agent to send the final response, reducing latency), and caps allocation at a maximum of 10 collaborator agents per supervisor. This is a concrete, vendor-documented bound on fan-out width for the allocate step of planning.
query: AWS Bedrock multi-agent collaboration supervisor task decomposition 2026
read: Creating a multi-agent collaboration comprises of the following steps: 1. Create and deploy collaborator agents. Make sure to configure each collaborator agent to implement a specific task within the multi-agent collaboration work flow. 2. Create a new supervisor agent or assign an existing agent the role of the supervisor... If you want supervisor agent to coordinate responses from the collaborator agents, select Supervisor. ... If you want supervisor agent to route information to the appropriate collaborator agent to send the final response, select Supervisor with routing. ... You can associate a maximum of 10 collaborator agents with a supervisor agent at this time.
snippet: You can assign the supervisor agent the task of coordinating responses from the collaborator agents or you can assign the supervisor agent the task of routing information to the appropriate collaborator agent to send the final response. Assigning the supervisor agent the task of routing information reduces the latency.
title: Create multi-agent collaboration - Amazon Bedrock
topic: Production multi-agent task decomposition: Amazon Bedrock supervisor agent decomposition and delegation modes

claim: Microsoft's Magentic orchestration (Agent Framework docs, ms.date 2026-09-04, built on the Magentic-One design) is a named, documented execution pattern offered alongside a simpler 'Group Chat orchestration' -- i.e. a real system where a caller selects between patterns. Its manager keeps a Task Ledger (facts/assumptions/plan) and a Progress Ledger (satisfied/in-loop/progressing/next-speaker), dynamically decomposes and delegates, and is bounded BEFORE a run completes by declared max_round_count, max_stall_count and max_reset_count builder parameters plus an optional human plan-signoff gate (RequirePlanSignoff) that pauses execution until a person approves or revises the proposed plan. This directly answers both the pattern-selection and the pre-execution-bounding parts of this research task from one primary, dated source.
query: Microsoft Magentic-One orchestrator task ledger decomposition agent 2026
read: The Magentic orchestration has the same architecture as the Group Chat orchestration pattern, with a very powerful manager that uses planning to coordinate agent collaboration. ... The builder also exposes the inner-loop limits (max coordination rounds, max consecutive stalls before replanning, max plan resets) and a flag for human-in-the-loop plan review... 1. Planning Phase: The manager analyzes the task and creates an initial plan 2. Optional Plan Review: If enabled, humans can review and approve/modify the plan 3. Agent Selection... 6. Stall Detection: If progress stalls, auto-replan with an optional human review process... A MagenticPlanReviewRequest carries the proposed plan, the current progress ledger... Build the response by calling either approve() to accept the plan as-is, or revise(...) with feedback to ask the manager to replan.
snippet: a dedicated Magentic manager coordinates a team of specialized agents, selecting which agent should act next based on the evolving context, task progress, and agent capabilities. The Magentic manager maintains a shared context, tracks progress, and adapts the workflow in real time. This enables the system to break down complex problems, delegate subtasks, and iteratively refine solutions through agent collaboration.
title: Microsoft Agent Framework Workflows Orchestrations - Magentic | Microsoft Learn
topic: Execution pattern taxonomy and pre-execution bounding: Microsoft Agent Framework's Magentic orchestration (task ledger, progress ledger, round/stall/reset limits, plan signoff)

claim: Anthropic's Building effective agents (published Dec 19, 2024) is the most widely cited published taxonomy of execution patterns a planner selects between -- prompt chaining (sequential pipeline), routing, parallelization (decomposition with parallel workers), orchestrator-workers (supervisor/worker, where 'subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input'), evaluator-optimizer, plus autonomous agents as a sixth, more open-ended category. Later 2026 sources found in this same pass (X-refmodel-2-3-planning-005, X-refmodel-2-3-planning-006) explicitly build on and echo this taxonomy. Published Dec 2024, older than this task's 2026-03 recency preference, but kept and flagged as the canonical original rather than excluded, per this task's own instruction that older canonical specs are fine if flagged.
query: Quote verbatim the text defining and naming the workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). Quote the definition of the orchestrator-workers pattern specifically, including any mention of dynamically decomposing tasks and delegating subtasks to workers. Note the publication date if shown.
read: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a sequence of steps, where each LLM call processes the output of the previous one. Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task. ... In the orchestrator-workers workflow, a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results. In the evaluator-optimizer workflow, one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop. ... the key difference from parallelization is its flexibility—subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.
snippet: In the orchestrator-workers workflow, a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results.
title: Building effective agents
topic: Canonical published taxonomy of agentic execution patterns a planner selects between

claim: A second 2026 taxonomy (Digital Applied, published Apr 30, 2026) organizes patterns into four quadrants and defines at least two of them in the page's own words -- ReAct as 'thought → action → observation, repeat' and Reflexion as 'ReAct + post-step self-critique'. Per the fetch summary (not itself a verbatim quote, so treated here as the record author's paraphrase of the page rather than as quoted text), the remaining quadrant labels are plan-and-execute, supervisor-worker, multi-agent debate, verifier-critic, graph orchestration and swarm/blackboard, with citations to Yao et al. 2022 (ReAct), Shinn et al. 2023 (Reflexion) and framework implementations (AutoGen, LangGraph). The page frames this as industry-converged vocabulary stabilized over 2024-2026 rather than crediting one org, corroborating that no single body owns the naming.

read:
Debate: multi-perspective critique, ~2.5× single-model cost.

Control flow. Two or more agents are given the same prompt, produce independent answers, and then either critique each other's outputs (the debate variant) or are evaluated by a separate judge model that selects the strongest answer and summarizes divergences (the Council variant). claim: This paper (arXiv 2604.22750v2, dated Apr 30, 2026) tests whether frontier models can predict their own token usage before executing an agentic coding task, and finds they cannot do so reliably: correlations between self-predicted and actual usage are only weak-to-moderate (up to 0.39), and models systematically underestimate real cost. This directly bounds what pricing a plan before execution can mean in practice -- asking the model itself for a cost estimate is a weak signal, which is why frameworks (X-refmodel-2-3-planning-003) bound plans with hard round/stall/reset limits rather than a computed price.
query: estimate cost steps before running agent plan token budget pre-execution 2026
read: frontier models fail to accurately predict their own token usage (with weak-to-moderate correlations, up to 0.39) and systematically underestimate real token costs.
snippet: Can agents predict their token usage before task execution?
title: How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? Analyzing and Predicting Token Consumption in Agentic Coding Tasks
topic: Agents cannot reliably self-estimate execution cost before running, undermining pre-execution pricing of a plan

claim: Opened May 3, 2026 by a Claude Code user (closed as duplicate, so the demand recurs), this issue is a concrete, dated statement of the priced-before-execution problem from a real product's users, who write that '"Run first, see cost later" is not acceptable in professional contexts.' It names three candidate mechanisms in order of preference -- calling a token-counting API on the plan content, a heuristic min/max range keyed to plan complexity (step count, tool calls, file operations), or a hard --max-tokens budget flag that aborts approval if the estimate exceeds it -- none of which is a computed guarantee, only an estimate surfaced at approval time.
query: estimate cost steps before running agent plan token budget pre-execution 2026
read: "Run first, see cost later" is not acceptable in professional contexts. Contractors quote before starting work. ... Implementation options (in order of preference): 1. API-based: Use the Anthropic count_tokens endpoint on the plan content before execution begins 2. Heuristic range: Show a conservative min/max based on plan complexity 3. Token budget flag: Allow --max-tokens <n> at plan approval; abort if estimate exceeds budget
snippet: When working with large or complex tasks in plan mode, there is currently no way to know — before approving — how many tokens the plan execution will consume.

claim: The A2A protocol specification (Latest Released Version 1.0.0), the field table for its Task object, has exactly six fields: id, contextId, status, artifacts, history, metadata -- none of them a decomposition, sub-task, or execution-plan field. Section 1.2 of the spec states its design principle as: agents 'collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations.' This is the finding for this task's fourth question: no open standard or published schema for a plan/task-decomposition document was found in this pass, and the one open, governance-backed standard covering agent task exchange keeps a task's internal plan explicitly out of the wire format by design, not by oversight.
query: Find the section defining the Task object's fields (the object with properties like id, contextId, status, artifacts, history, metadata). Reproduce that field table or field list verbatim, row by row, exactly as written on the page -- field name, type, required, and description for each field. Also quote verbatim any sentence in the spec that describes tasks as atomic/opaque or that explicitly says the protocol does not model task decomposition, sub-tasks, or execution plans.
read: id string Yes Unique identifier (e.g. UUID) for the task, generated by the server for a new task. | contextId string No Unique identifier (e.g. UUID) for the contextual collection of interactions (tasks and messages). | status TaskStatus Yes The current status of a Task, including state and a message. | artifacts array of Artifact No A set of output artifacts for a Task. | history array of Message No The history of interactions from a Task. | metadata object No A key/value object to store custom metadata about a task. ... Agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations.
snippet: Agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations.
